units.title: Loops
units.summary: Iteration in C++: increment and decrement operators, while, do-while and for loops, counters, accumulators, sentinels, nested loops, break and continue, and a light look at file streams.

lessons.title: Increment and decrement operators
lessons.html:
The increment operator ++ adds 1 to its operand and the decrement operator -- subtracts 1. The operand must be a modifiable variable (an lvalue).

Each has two forms. In prefix mode (++x) the variable changes first and the expression's value is the new value. In postfix mode (x++) the expression's value is the old value, and the variable changes afterward.

int x = 5;
int a = x++;   // a is 5, x is 6
int b = ++x;   // x is 7, b is 7
int c = x--;   // c is 7, x is 6
int d = --x;   // x is 5, d is 5

Used as a stand-alone statement, x++; and ++x; do exactly the same thing. The difference only shows when the value of the expression is used, such as in an assignment, a test or an output statement.

Precedence and traps

  • Postfix and prefix ++ and -- have higher precedence than arithmetic: n-- - 3 uses the old n in the subtraction.
  • Modifying one variable more than once in a single expression, such as i++ + ++i or n * n++, is undefined behavior: there is no reliable result. Keep to one modification per statement.
  • In a relational test, postfix compares the old value: while (t++ < 3) tests 0, 1, 2, 3 and leaves t at 4. Prefix compares the new value.
  • The operand must be a variable: ++(a + b) and 5++ do not compile.
  • ++ and -- are also used in loop counters and the update part of a for loop, where only the side effect matters.
FormValue of the expressionFinal x
y = x++ (x is 5)56
y = ++x (x is 5)66

Compound assignments like x += 2 are the usual way to step by amounts other than 1.

lessons.title: The while loop, input validation and counters
lessons.html:
A loop repeats a block of statements. The while loop has the form while (condition) statement;. The first line is the loop header; the statement or block it repeats is the body, also called a conditionally executed statement because it runs only while the condition is true. The condition is tested first. If it is true the body runs, then the condition is tested again. If it is false from the start, the body never runs. That is why while is a pretest loop. One pass through the body is an iteration. A variable that the condition tests and the body changes, like n below, is the loop control variable.

int n = 1;
while (n <= 3) {
    cout << n << " ";
    n++;
}                    // prints 1 2 3

A body made of several statements needs braces. Without them only the first statement after the condition is in the loop.

Infinite loops

A loop whose condition never becomes false is an infinite loop. Typical causes: forgetting to change the variable the condition tests, a semicolon right after while (...) (an empty body), using = where == was meant, and testing equality with != or == when a step can jump over the target value (i != 10 while adding 3).

Input validation

Read a value before the loop (the priming read), then loop while it is invalid, prompting and reading again inside:

cin >> age;
while (age < 0 || age > 120) {
    cout << "Try again: ";
    cin >> age;
}

Counters

A counter is a variable that goes up or down by a fixed step on every iteration to track how many times something happened. Initialize it before the loop; an uninitialized local variable holds garbage, not 0. Counting can also be done by 2, 5, or -1; the step does not have to be 1.

Pseudocode maps directly: While count < 3: display, add 1 becomes a while with braces holding both steps. In a flowchart, a while is a diamond at the top whose Yes branch goes through the body and back to the diamond.

lessons.title: The do-while loop
lessons.html:
The do-while loop tests after the body, so it is a posttest loop. The body always executes at least once.

do {
    cout << "Enter a number: ";
    cin >> num;
} while (num < 0);     // required semicolon

The semicolon after the closing parenthesis is required. A while loop is the opposite: no semicolon after its condition (adding one makes the body empty).

whiledo-while
Testbefore bodyafter body
Minimum runs01
Semicolon at endnoyes

Equivalence

If the starting values make the condition true on entry, a while and a do-while with the same body behave the same. Otherwise they differ: with int i = 5; while (i < 5) the body is skipped; with do ... while (i < 5) it runs once. A do-while is the same as one unconditional copy of the body followed by a while loop.

When to choose it

Use it when something must happen before it can be tested: menus, "run again?" prompts, password entry. A loop that goes around until the user chooses to quit (while (again == 'y')) is a user-controlled loop. In pseudocode, Repeat ... Until cond is a posttest loop that stops when cond becomes true, so it becomes do { ... } while (!(cond)); with the test reversed. Be careful with sentinels: do { cin >> n; sum += n; } while (n != -1); adds the sentinel to the total, because the test comes after the addition.

Flowchart shape

In a flowchart a do-while is recognized because the process boxes come first and the decision diamond is at the bottom, with its Yes branch looping back up to the start of the body. A while loop's diamond is at the top.

Tracing tip: write the variable's value at each test, and count tests, not just body runs. A do-while with n++ and test n < 5 starting at 10 still prints 10 once.

lessons.title: The for loop
lessons.html:
A conditional loop repeats while a condition holds (input validation), so its number of iterations is not known in advance. A count-controlled loop repeats a known number of times and needs three things: initialize a counter, test it against a limit, update it each iteration. The for loop packs those three parts into one header:

for (initialization; test; update)
    statement;
  1. The initialization expression runs once, before anything else.
  2. The test expression is evaluated before every iteration, including the first. If false, the loop ends. So a for is a pretest loop.
  3. The body runs, then the update expression runs, then back to the test.
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)      // i = 0,1,2,3 : 4 iterations
    cout << i;

It is equivalent to int i = 0; while (i < 4) { cout << i; i++; }.

What each part may contain

  • Initialization and update may hold several expressions separated by commas: for (int lo = 0, hi = 9; lo < hi; lo++, hi--). The test is one expression.
  • Any part may be omitted, but both semicolons stay. for (;;) loops forever unless break or return stops it. An omitted test counts as true.
  • Counting down: for (int i = 10; i >= 1; i--). Other steps: i += 5, i *= 2.

Scope

A variable declared in the initialization (int i = 0) exists only in the loop. Using it after the loop is a compile error. To use the final value afterward, declare the variable before the loop.

Traps

  • A semicolon after the header gives an empty body: for (...); then the next statement runs once.
  • Number of iterations of for (i = a; i < b; i++) is b - a (when a is at most b). With <= it is b - a + 1. With a step s, count the values visited.
  • Change the counter only in the update expression. Changing it in the body too (an extra i++) makes the loop skip values and stop at an unexpected point.
  • Variables may be defined inside the body, but they exist only inside that block.

lessons.title: Accumulators, sentinels and choosing a loop
lessons.html:
A running total is a sum that gets bigger every time the loop body runs. The variable that holds it is an accumulator. It must be initialized before the loop, almost always to 0 for sums and to 1 for products. An uninitialized accumulator starts with garbage.

int sum = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++)
    sum += i * i;          // 1+4+9+16+25 = 55

For an average, divide the sum by the count. With two int variables the division truncates: 17 / 4 is 4, not 4.25. Cast one operand to double to keep the fraction.

Sentinels

A sentinel is a special value, impossible as real data, that tells the loop to stop. Read with a priming read so the sentinel is tested before it is processed:

cin >> n;
while (n != -1) {
    sum += n;
    cin >> n;
}

Putting the add inside a do-while before the test processes the sentinel too, a classic mistake.

Which loop?

  • for: you know the number of iterations or a range of values to step through.
  • while: the loop may need to run zero times, such as validating input or reading until a sentinel.
  • do-while: the body must run at least once, such as menus and "again?" prompts.

All three are interchangeable in power; choosing is about clarity. Also note both while and for are pretest loops, so either may run zero times.

The book (5.9) sums it up: while and do-while are conditional loops, good for validation, sentinel lists (while) and menus (do-while); for is the pretest loop with built-in initialize, test and update, ideal when the precise pass count is known in advance. When an algorithm is given in pseudocode, find its initialization, test and update and place them in whichever form fits.

lessons.title: Nested loops, break and continue
lessons.book: Sections 5.10 and 5.12, pages 272 to 275 and 294 to 296
lessons.html:
A nested loop is a loop inside another. Each time the outer loop goes around once, the inner loop begins again from its start and finishes all of its passes. The inner body runs outer count times inner count in total.

for (int r = 1; r <= 3; r++) {      // 3 rows
    for (int c = 1; c <= r; c++)    // inner count depends on r
        cout << '*';
    cout << '\n';
}                                   // 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 stars

If the inner limit depends on the outer variable, add the inner counts instead of multiplying: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 for limits 1 to 4. The inner loop's counter changes fastest, like the second hand of a clock. Use different variable names for each loop (i, j). Reusing the same counter breaks both loops.

break

break immediately leaves the innermost loop (or switch) containing it. Execution continues with the statement after that loop. In nested loops, the outer loop keeps going.

continue

continue skips the rest of the current iteration and goes on to the next one. In a for, control goes to the update expression, then the test. In a while or do-while, control goes directly to the test, so if the update was skipped by the continue the loop can run forever.

for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
    if (i % 2 == 0) continue;   // skip evens
    cout << i;                  // 135
}
int i = 0;
while (i < 5) {
    if (i == 2) continue;       // BUG: i++ is skipped, infinite
    i++;
}

Tracing nested loops: write a table with a column per variable and one row per inner test. Count the final values of loop variables carefully: after a normal exit from for (i = 1; i <= 3; i++), i is 4. After a break, i keeps the value it had when break ran.

lessons.title: Reading and writing files (not on syllabus)
lessons.html:
This section is outside the course syllabus; know the vocabulary only.

File streams come from the header <fstream>. ofstream writes to a file (output file stream), ifstream reads from one (input file stream). You can use << and >> on them just as with cout and cin.

#include <fstream>
ofstream out;
out.open("scores.txt");   // creates the file, or erases an existing one
out << 90 << endl;
out.close();

ifstream in("scores.txt");
int v;
while (in >> v)           // false at end of file or a failed read
    cout << v;
in.close();

open connects the stream to a file. Opening an existing file with an ofstream erases its old contents. An input file keeps a read position, the next byte to be read; it starts at the beginning of the file and moves forward with each read. close disconnects it and flushes buffered output. An input stream cannot read a file that does not exist, so check that the open succeeded (for example if (!in)). The idiom while (in >> v) reads until end of file because the extraction expression becomes false when no value could be read.

Files are one way to supply data to loops: a sum or search loop works the same whether it reads from cin or from a file stream.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: Postfix `x++` yields the old value (5) for `y`, then x becomes 6. So x is 6 and y is 5.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: `a++ * 2` uses 4 then a becomes 5, so b is 8. `++a` makes a 6 first, so c is 12. Final a is 6.

questions.prompt: After this code runs, what are the values of n and m?
choices: n is 9 and m is 7
n is 10 and m is 7
n is 9 and m is 6
n is 10 and m is 6
questions.explain: `n--` yields the old value 10 in the expression, so m = 10 - 3 = 7. The decrement still happens afterward, leaving n at 9.

questions.prompt: As complete statements by themselves, `count++;` and `++count;` have exactly the same effect on count.
questions.explain: The prefix/postfix difference matters only when the expression's value is used. Standing alone, both just add 1.

questions.prompt: The `--` operator is called the ____ operator.
questions.explain: `--` subtracts 1 from its operand; `++` is the increment operator.

questions.prompt: Why is the statement `int r = i++ + ++i;` a bad idea?
choices: Postfix and prefix operators cannot appear in the same statement by rule of syntax
It modifies i twice in one expression with no defined order, so the result is not reliable
It always evaluates to 0
It is fine; C++ evaluates strictly left to right so the result is well-defined
questions.explain: Changing the same variable more than once in one expression without sequencing is undefined behavior. Use one modification per statement.

questions.prompt: The statement `5++;` is legal because 5 is a value that can be increased.
questions.explain: The operand of ++ and -- must be a modifiable variable (an lvalue). A literal cannot be changed.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The body runs for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, printing the squares 1 4 9 16. When n becomes 5 the test fails and the loop exits, then end prints.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body of this loop run?
choices: It is an infinite loop
questions.explain: while tests first. k > 10 is false when k is 10, so the body never runs. That is the meaning of a pretest loop.

questions.prompt: A while loop is a pretest loop: its condition is evaluated before each execution of the body, so the body might never execute.
questions.explain: Contrast with do-while, which tests after the body and always runs at least once.

questions.prompt: Why does this program never finish?
choices: i is declared as int instead of unsigned
The braces must come before the condition
cout cannot be used inside a while loop
The semicolon after the condition makes the loop body empty, so i never changes
questions.explain: `while (i < 5);` loops on an empty statement forever. The block after it is a separate statement that is never reached.

questions.prompt: What does this program print?
choices: done
hihihi... forever
hidone
The code does not compile
questions.explain: `x = 0` is an assignment, not a comparison. It stores 0 in x and the expression's value is 0, which is false, so the body is skipped.

questions.prompt: The user types 120, then -5, then 88. What does this program print?
questions.explain: The first two entries are out of range, so bad prints twice. The third passes the test, the loop ends, and 88 prints. The first read before the loop is the priming read.

questions.prompt: In an input validation loop, why is the first value read BEFORE the while statement?
choices: while loops cannot contain cin
The condition needs a value to test before the loop can decide whether to run
It makes the loop run faster
The value must be read twice to be stored
questions.explain: The priming read gives the condition something to examine. The loop body then re-reads inside, so each new value is tested before it is used.

questions.prompt: The only statement in a loop body that touches `passes` is `passes++;`, and `passes` starts at 0. After the loop, it tells how many times the body ran. What is this kind of variable called?
questions.explain: A counter is usually initialized to 0 (or a start value) before the loop and changed by a fixed amount each iteration.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: n goes 100, 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1 using integer division. That is 6 divisions, so c is 6, and the loop stops when n is 1.

questions.prompt: What happens when this loop runs?
choices: It stops when i equals 10
It stops after 4 iterations
It never stops, because i jumps from 9 to 12 and never equals 10
It does not compile because != is invalid in a while
questions.explain: i takes 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, ... and the test `i != 10` is always true. Use a relational test like `i < 10` when stepping by more than 1.

questions.prompt: If a while loop's body has two statements and the braces are left off, both statements are still part of the loop.
questions.explain: Without braces only the single statement right after the condition belongs to the loop. The second statement runs once, after the loop ends. Indenting it does not change this; the compiler ignores indentation.

questions.prompt:
Pseudocode:
Set count to 0
While count < 3
  Display count * 2
  Add 1 to count
Which C++ matches it?
questions.explain: It prints 0 2 4. The wrong choices drop the braces (infinite loop), use <= (one extra pass), or start at 1 (misses the first value).

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The body runs once before the condition is tested. It prints 10, then 11 < 5 is false and the loop ends.

questions.prompt: The do-while loop is called a ____ loop because it tests its condition after the body.
questions.explain: Because the test comes last, the body of a do-while always runs at least once.

questions.prompt: A do-while statement must end with a semicolon after the closing parenthesis of its condition.
questions.explain: `do { ... } while (cond);` The semicolon is required; leaving it off is a syntax error.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this loop?
choices: There is no semicolon after the while condition
The body should not use braces
The condition must come before the word do
x++ cannot be used in a do-while
questions.explain: A do-while must end with `;`. Compare with a while loop, which must NOT have a semicolon after its condition.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum number of times the body of a do-while loop executes?
choices: It depends on the condition
questions.explain: The body runs first and the test happens afterward, so at least one pass is guaranteed.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The while loop does not run (5 < 5 is false). The do-while prints B once and increments i to 6. Then 6 is printed, giving B6.

questions.prompt: A program shows a menu and must display it at least once before testing whether the user chose Quit. Which loop fits best?
choices: while
a for loop that repeats exactly 5 times
do-while
a nested loop
questions.explain: A posttest loop guarantees the first pass, so the menu appears before the test. A while would need a duplicated first display or a priming trick.

questions.prompt: Which loop does exactly the same thing as the do-while below for ANY starting value of k?
choices: while (k < 6) { cout << k; k += 2; }
while (k < 6) { k += 2; cout << k; }
do { k += 2; cout << k; } while (k < 6);

cout << k; k += 2;
while (k < 6) { cout << k; k += 2; }
questions.explain: A do-while is a while loop whose body is run once unconditionally first. Only the choice that writes the body once before a while loop does this. The plain while skips the body when k starts at 6 or more, and the others change the order of the statements.

questions.prompt: A flowchart is described this way: Start, set n to 3, process box Display n, process box Subtract 1 from n, diamond 'n > 0?' with Yes going back to Display n and No going to End. Which C++ matches?
questions.explain: The decision comes after the process boxes, which is the shape of a do-while. It prints 3 2 1. The pretest version that decrements first prints 2 1 0, the version with a semicolon after `while (n > 0)` loops forever, and the version testing `n < 0` ends after one pass.

questions.prompt: The second expression in a for loop header, which decides whether the body runs again, is called the ____ expression.
questions.explain: A for header holds initialization; test; update. The test is evaluated before every iteration, like a while condition.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.code:
for (int i = 2; i <= 10; i += 4)
    cout << i << " ";
questions.explain: i takes 2, 6, 10 (10 <= 10 is true), then 14 which fails the test.

questions.prompt: How many times does the body of this loop run?
questions.explain: i is 0, 3, 6, 9, and 12 fails i < 10. That is 4 iterations.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The loop counts down 3, 2, 1 and stops when i reaches 0. Then Go prints.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
questions.code:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { }
cout << i;
choices: It prints 3
It prints 2
It does not compile, because i is out of scope after the loop
It prints 0
questions.explain: A variable declared in the for header exists only inside the loop. The cout after the loop cannot see i.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: x is declared outside, so it survives the loop. It goes 0, 6, 12, 18, 24. At 24 the test fails, so 24 prints.

questions.prompt: All three expressions in a for loop header are optional, and `for (;;)` is a loop that runs until something like break stops it.
questions.explain: An omitted test is treated as true. The two semicolons are still required.

questions.prompt: Which while loop prints exactly the same thing as `for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) cout << i << " ";`?
questions.explain: The initialization goes before the loop and the update goes at the end of the body, so it prints 1 2 3 4 5. Updating first prints 2 3 4 5 6, starting at 0 prints an extra 0, and the do-while testing `i < 5` stops after 4.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.code:
for (int lo = 0, hi = 5; lo < hi; lo++, hi--)
    cout << lo << hi << " ";
questions.explain: The comma lets the header initialize and update two variables. Pairs: (0,5), (1,4), (2,3). Next is (3,2), where 3 < 2 is false.

questions.prompt: How many times does the statement `count++;` run? (The program prints count at the end.)
choices: It is an infinite loop
questions.explain: The semicolon right after the header is the loop body (an empty statement). The loop runs 3 times doing nothing, then `count++;` runs once, after the loop. The indentation is misleading; the compiler ignores it.

questions.prompt: Which header displays 10 9 8 ... 3 2 1 when the body is `cout << i << " ";`?
choices: for (int i = 10; i > 1; i--)
for (int i = 10; i >= 1; i--)
for (int i = 10; i <= 1; i--)
for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i--)
questions.explain: Counting down to 1 needs a decrement and a test that is still true at 1, such as `i >= 1`. With `i > 1` the loop stops before printing 1; with `i <= 1` the test is false at the start so nothing prints; starting at 1 and decrementing moves away from 10, so that test never fails.

questions.prompt:
Complete the header so it visits 0, 5, 10, ... 100:
`for (int n = 0; n <= 100; ____)`
questions.explain: The update expression adds 5 each pass, which stays within the test limit of 100.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: Initialization and update are omitted here, which is legal. j goes 1, 3, 9, 27, 81. At 81 the test fails.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The accumulator adds 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 = 55.

questions.prompt: This loop multiplies the numbers 1 through 5 into prod, which should end up holding 120. What should fill the blank?
choices: Any value; it will be overwritten
questions.explain: An accumulator for a product starts at 1, the value that does not change a product. Start at 0 and the product stays 0 forever; leave it uninitialized and it starts with garbage. Starting at 1 gives 1 x 2 x 3 x 4 x 5 = 120.

questions.prompt: A special value that signals the end of a list of input values and is not treated as real data is called a ____.
questions.explain: The loop tests for it; it must be a value that can never be valid data, such as -1 for an age.

questions.prompt: The user enters 4 9 2 -1. What does this program print?
questions.explain: The sentinel -1 ends the loop before it is added. The sum is 4 + 9 + 2 = 15.

questions.prompt: The user enters 4 9 2 -1. What does this program print?
questions.explain: This do-while adds each value before testing it, including the sentinel. 4 + 9 + 2 + (-1) = 14. The while version with a priming read avoids this.

questions.prompt: Like a while loop, a for loop whose condition is false at the very start runs its body zero times.
questions.explain: A for loop evaluates its test before the first iteration, so the body can run zero times.

questions.prompt: A variable that keeps a running total by having each new value added to it is called an ____.
questions.explain: The sum itself is the running total; the variable that holds it is the accumulator. It must be initialized (usually to 0) before the loop starts.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: For each i the inner loop runs j = 1 and 2. Row 1: 1 2, row 2: 2 4, row 3: 3 6.

questions.prompt: How many times does the statement `count++;` run? (The program prints count at the end.)
questions.explain: The inner loop runs completely, 3 times, for each of the 4 outer iterations. Multiply, do not add: 4 x 3 = 12.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The inner loop runs 1, 2, 3, then 4 times: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: Row r prints r stars, giving a triangle of 1, 2 and 3 stars.

questions.prompt: An outer loop runs 4 times and, on each of those passes, an inner loop runs 3 times. The inner loop's body therefore executes 7 times in total.
questions.explain: The inner loop starts over and completes for every outer pass, so the counts multiply: 4 * 3 = 12, not 4 + 3.

questions.prompt: The statement that immediately ends the innermost loop containing it is ____.
questions.explain: Execution continues with the first statement after that loop.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: continue skips the rest of the body for even values, so only 1, 3 and 5 print.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: At i = 6, 36 > 30 triggers break before last is updated, and i is not incremented again. So last is 5 and i is 6.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: break leaves only the inner loop. Each time the outer loop runs, j = 1 prints and j = 2 breaks. The outer loop still goes on to i = 2 and 3.

questions.prompt: What happens when this loop runs?
choices: It never ends, because when i is 2 the continue skips i++
It prints nothing and ends
It ends when i reaches 5
It ends after skipping the value 2
questions.explain: continue in a while loop jumps straight to the condition test. With i stuck at 2, the same path repeats forever.

questions.prompt: In a for loop, the continue statement skips the update expression, so i is not incremented on that pass.
questions.explain: continue jumps to the update expression of a for loop, then the test. That is a major difference from while, where there is no automatic update.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `break` inside nested loops is correct?
choices: It exits all enclosing loops
It exits only the innermost loop that contains it
It skips the current iteration of the outer loop only
It restarts the inner loop from its initialization
questions.explain: break exits the one loop it is directly inside. Leaving several loops needs a flag, a return, or a goto.

questions.prompt: Which header must be included to use ifstream and ofstream?
questions.explain: Both classes are declared in the `<fstream>` header.

questions.prompt: Which type should you declare to write data into a file?
choices: ifstream
istream
ofstream
iostream
questions.explain: The o stands for output: an ofstream writes to a file. ifstream reads from a file, and istream and iostream are the console stream types used by cin and cout.

questions.prompt: After you finish using a file stream you should call its `close` member function.
questions.explain: Closing flushes any buffered data and releases the file.

questions.prompt: Which loop reads integers from the ifstream inFile until the end of the file is reached?
choices: while (inFile.close()) { ... }
while (value != EOF) { cin >> value; }
for (;;) { inFile << value; }
while (inFile >> value) { ... }
questions.explain: The extraction expression evaluates to false when a read fails, including at end of file, so the loop ends naturally.

questions.prompt: If an ofstream opens a file name that does not exist yet, the file is created; if an ifstream opens a file name that does not exist, the open fails.
questions.explain: An output stream creates the file it is asked to open. An input stream cannot read a file that is not there, so check that the open worked, for example with `if (!inFile)`, before reading.

questions.prompt: The statement or block of statements that a loop repeats is called the ____ of the loop.
questions.explain: The first line, such as `while (count < 10)`, is the loop header; what it repeats is the body. The body is a conditionally executed statement, because it runs only while the condition is true.

questions.prompt: One pass through the body of a loop is called an ____.
questions.explain: A loop whose body runs 7 times performs 7 iterations. "How many times does the loop run" asks for the number of iterations.

questions.prompt: A loop that has no way of stopping, because its condition never becomes false, is called an ____ loop.
questions.explain: Common causes: never changing the variable the condition tests, a semicolon right after `while (...)`, and using `=` where `==` was meant.

questions.prompt: When ++ or -- is written before its operand, as in `++total`, the operator is being used in ____ mode.
questions.explain: Prefix mode changes the variable first and then uses the new value. Postfix mode (`total++`) uses the old value and changes the variable afterward.

questions.prompt: A loop keeps asking for a password and ends only when the correct one is typed. Nobody can say beforehand how many passes it will make. Which term describes it best?
choices: count-controlled loop
conditional loop
nested loop
counter-limited for loop
questions.explain: A conditional loop repeats while (or until) a condition holds, so its number of passes is not known in advance. A count-controlled loop initializes a counter, tests it against a limit and updates it, which suits a repeat count fixed before the loop starts.

questions.prompt: A program must process exactly 30 test scores, one per iteration. Which loop is the best fit?
choices: while
do-while
a nested loop
for
questions.explain: The for loop is ideal when you can say in advance exactly how many passes are needed: its header initializes, tests and updates the counter in one place. A while could do it, but the for is the tool the book recommends for counting.

questions.prompt: A program reads numbers until the user enters -1. If -1 is the very first number entered, the processing step must not run at all. Which loop fits best?
choices: a do-while loop that reads and processes, then tests
a while loop with a priming read before it
a for loop that always runs exactly 10 times
a nested loop
questions.explain: A while loop is a pretest loop, so with a priming read it can stop before processing anything. A do-while always processes at least once, so it would process the -1 too.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: Each pass adds 2 in the body and 1 in the update, so i goes 0, 3, 6, 9, then 12 fails the test. This is why the book warns against changing a for loop's counter inside the body: the loop stops at unexpected values.

questions.prompt: A counter does not need to be initialized before a loop, because `count++` starts an uninitialized int variable at 0.
questions.explain: A local variable that is not initialized holds an unpredictable value, and reading it is undefined behavior. Always set a counter (and an accumulator) to its starting value before the loop.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: Postfix compares the OLD value and then increments. The tests use 0, 1, 2 (true, printing 1 2 3) and then 3 (false), but t is still incremented to 4 by that last test.

questions.prompt: What happens with this code?
choices: It prints 10
It increments a, then prints 10
It does not compile, because the operand of ++ must be a variable, not an expression such as (a + b)
It increments both a and b, then prints 11
questions.explain: ++ and -- need something that can be changed (an lvalue). `a + b` is a temporary value with no storage to update, so g++ reports "lvalue required as increment operand". Write `c = a + b + 1;` instead.

questions.prompt: This loop should let the user add numbers and repeat while they answer y. What is the main logic error?
choices: again is tested before it has ever been given a value; a do-while (or reading again before the loop) fixes it
a char cannot be compared with == to a character literal
total must be declared inside the loop
the condition should use && instead of ||
questions.explain: The first test reads an uninitialized variable, so whether the body runs at all is unpredictable. A do-while runs the body once before testing again, which is the natural fit for a "do this again?" loop. The || is correct: either y or Y should repeat.

questions.prompt: This loop is meant to add up howMany numbers. The user enters 4, then 10 20 30 40. What does it print?
questions.explain: i is increased in the body AND in the update, so it goes 0, 2, 4 and only two numbers (10 and 20) are read. Change the counter only in the update expression. Declaring num inside the body is fine.

questions.prompt: The user enters 0 at the prompt. What happens?
choices: The loop ends, because choice is 0
It does not compile, because = cannot appear in a condition
The loop ends, because a do-while always runs exactly once
The loop runs again, and keeps running whatever is entered
questions.explain: `choice = 1` assigns 1 to choice, and the value of that expression is 1, which is true. So the test is always true and the loop never ends. The fix is `choice == 1`. It does compile; g++ only warns.

questions.prompt: A variable defined inside the body of a while loop can still be used by statements after the loop ends.
questions.explain: Defining variables inside a loop body is allowed, but their scope is that block. After the closing brace the name no longer exists, so using it is a compile error.

questions.prompt: In a nested loop, the outer loop's counter changes value more often than the inner loop's counter.
questions.explain: It is the other way around. The inner loop runs all of its iterations for each single iteration of the outer loop, like a clock's second hand moving 60 times for each move of the minute hand.

questions.prompt: The break statement skips the rest of the current iteration and then continues with the loop's next iteration.
questions.explain: That describes continue. break ends the loop immediately, and execution goes to the first statement after the loop.

questions.prompt: Inside a loop body, which keyword abandons the rest of the current pass and sends control on to the next pass of the same loop?
questions.explain: In a while or do-while, continue jumps to the test; in a for, it jumps to the update expression and then the test. break, by contrast, leaves the loop.

questions.prompt: By default, opening a file that already exists with an ofstream object erases the file's previous contents.
questions.explain: An ofstream opened in its default mode starts the file empty, so old data is lost. Appending instead needs a different open mode, which this course does not require.

questions.prompt: When an ifstream object first opens a file for reading, where is the file's read position?
choices: At the end of the file
Wherever the last program that used the file stopped
At the first byte of the file
In the middle of the file
questions.explain: The read position marks the next byte to be read. It starts at the beginning of the file and moves forward as each value is read.

questions.prompt: In this loop, which part runs exactly once, no matter how many times the loop iterates?
questions.code:
for (int k = 0; k < 8; k++)
    total += k;
choices: `total += k`
`int k = 0`
questions.explain: The initialization expression runs once, before anything else. Here the test is evaluated 9 times (the last one fails), and the body and the update each run 8 times.

questions.prompt: The user enters 4, then 10 20 5 -3. What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The user chooses how many times the for loop runs (a user-controlled loop). It reads 4 values and adds them: 10 + 20 + 5 - 3 = 32. A negative value is just data here, because the loop counts rather than watching for a sentinel.

questions.prompt: The user enters y, then Y, then n. What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The body runs once before the first test, then again after y and after Y. The n makes the test false. This is a user-controlled loop: the user decides when it stops.

questions.prompt: What does this pseudocode display?
questions.code:
Set total to 0
Set k to 1
While k <= 9
    Add k to total
    Add 2 to k
End While
Display total
questions.explain: k takes the values 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11 fails the test. The total is 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25.

questions.prompt: Which C++ matches this pseudocode? (Repeat ... Until runs the body first and stops when its condition becomes true.)
questions.code:
Set n to 1
Repeat
    Display n
    Set n to n * 3
Until n > 50
choices:
for (int n = 1; n > 50; n *= 3)
    cout << n << " ";
questions.explain: "Until n > 50" means keep going while n <= 50, and the body comes first, so it is a do-while with the opposite test. It prints 1 3 9 27. Copying the Until test unchanged stops after printing 1, multiplying first prints 3 9 27 81, and the for loop never runs.

questions.prompt: A flowchart: Start, then a process box "Set x to 20", then a diamond "x > 2?". The Yes branch goes to "Display x", then "Set x to x / 2" (integer division), then back to the diamond. The No branch goes to End. What is displayed?
questions.explain: The diamond is at the top, so this is a while loop. x is 20, 10 and 5 when tested true and displayed; then 5 / 2 is 2, and 2 > 2 is false, so 2 is never displayed.

questions.prompt: Which flowchart description matches this loop?
questions.code:
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
    cout << i;
choices: Set i to 1; diamond "i < 3?"; Yes: Display i, Add 1 to i, back to the diamond; No: End
Set i to 1; diamond "i <= 3?"; Yes: Add 1 to i, Display i, back to the diamond; No: End
Set i to 1; diamond "i <= 3?"; Yes: Display i, Add 1 to i, back to the diamond; No: End
Set i to 0; diamond "i <= 3?"; Yes: Display i, Add 1 to i, back to the diamond; No: End
questions.explain: A for loop is a pretest loop: initialize once, test in a diamond, run the body, then the update, then back to the test. It prints 123. Testing i < 3 prints 12, updating before displaying prints 234, and starting at 0 prints 0123.

questions.prompt: The user enters 6, -2, 9, 0, 4. What does this pseudocode display?
questions.code:
Set sum to 0
Input value
While value is not 0
    Add value to sum
    Input value
End While
Display sum
questions.explain: 0 is the sentinel. The loop adds 6, -2 and 9 (13), stops when it reads 0, and never reads the 4. The input before the loop is the priming read.

questions.prompt: Which C++ matches this pseudocode?
questions.code:
For row from 1 to 3
    For col from 1 to row
        Display col
    End For
    Start a new line
End For
questions.explain: "From 1 to row" includes row, so the inner test is `col <= row`, and the new line belongs to the outer loop, after the inner loop ends. The result is 1, 12, 123 on three lines. Using 3 prints 123 three times, `col < row` drops the last number, and moving endl inside puts every number on its own line.

questions.prompt: What does this program segment print?
questions.explain: The update happens in the condition (`v++`), so continue cannot skip it and the loop still ends. The body sees v = 1 to 6 and skips 3 and 6.

questions.prompt: The variable that a loop's condition tests and the body changes, so that it decides how many times the loop runs, is called the loop ____ variable.
questions.explain: In `while (n <= 5) { ...; n++; }`, n is the loop control variable. If the body never changes it, the loop is infinite.

questions.prompt: In an input validation loop, the input statement placed just before the loop, which gives the condition its first value to test, is called the ____.
questions.explain: The priming read gets the first value; a second read at the end of the body gets each later value, so every value is tested before it is used.

questions.prompt: A sum of numbers that grows with each iteration of a loop is called a ____.
questions.explain: The running total is the sum itself; the variable that holds it is the accumulator.

programs.title: Sentinel average
programs.task: Read integers until the user enters 0 (the sentinel; do not count it). Print how many numbers were entered, their sum, and their average with 2 decimal places on separate lines, labeled Count, Sum and Average. If no numbers were entered, print only 'No data'.

programs.title: Validated multiplication table
programs.task: Ask for a table size from 1 to 9, repeating the prompt 'Size (1-9):' on its own line until valid. Then print a size x size multiplication table, one row per line, numbers separated by single spaces.

programs.title: Number triangle
programs.task: Read n. Print a triangle in which row r (1 to n) contains the numbers 1 to r separated by single spaces. Use nested for loops.

programs.title: Collatz steps
programs.task: Read a positive integer n. Print the sequence, starting with n and separated by spaces, using these rules until n reaches 1: if n is even, halve it; if odd, replace it with 3n + 1. Then on a new line print 'Steps: ' and the number of changes made.

programs.title: Skip, stop and total
programs.task: Read 10 integers with a for loop. Ignore negative numbers (continue). Stop reading at the first 0 (break). Print the count of positive numbers processed, their sum and the largest, each on its own line, labeled Count, Sum and Largest.
